summary:
With today's 4.3 psi spacesuits, a Moon base cannot both spare its crew the pure-oxygen prebreathe before every spacewalk and keep its air where small fires go out on their own. Airburn shows this with NASA's own data. NASA's FLEX droplet-fire tests put the burn line at 20.4 to 23.4% oxygen: in ISS air 17 of 32 burning droplets went out on their own, at Moon-base oxygen 2 of 23. NASA's decompression and breathing limits mean no cabin below 27.6% oxygen skips the prebreathe, past that line. The fix is the suit: at 5.8 psi, the pressure of Russia's Orlan suit, a Moon base could skip the prebreathe at 21.7% oxygen, where 67% of droplet flames go out on their own instead of 14%.

Airburn is the SI-powered dashboard behind this. It turns 1,989 test records from 21 NASA PSI tables into one table, ranks nine fire-safety findings for any habitat, has SI interpret each one with every sentence checked, predicts outcomes with uncertainty, replays NASA's tests, and adds results from seven NASA technical reports. The air for the first Moon bases is being chosen now, and that choice is a fire-safety decision.
details:
What it does. You describe a habitat (oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity, the materials on board) or start from the ISS, a Moon base, NASA's exploration atmosphere or a spacesuit. Airburn then:

1. Chooses the air. For any cabin oxygen and pressure, and a suit pressure from today's 4.3 psi to the 8.2 psi of NASA's xEMU design, it shows how long the pure-oxygen prebreathe before a spacewalk is, how the oxygen compares with what NASA accepts, the chance a burning droplet goes out on its own, and the NASA tests nearby, on one chart with the crew atmospheres. Every briefing carries the same numbers in one line, and live SI can cite them.

2. Ranks what NASA's experiments found. Code computes nine findings from the outcome columns of the NASA tables: how often droplet and gas flames went out on their own at each oxygen level, what CO2 and helium did, cool flames, what gravity changed, flame spread with and against the airflow, carbon monoxide from burning samples, and smoke. Each is ranked for your habitat by Relevance = C_oxygen × ½(1 + C_pressure) × W_tests, which scores how close its tests came to your conditions. A one-word badge (Tested, Sparse, Untested) says how many tests sit near your atmosphere.

3. Interprets them with SI. For each finding, SI writes a headline, what the tests found, what it suggests for a crewed habitat and its main limit, plus a briefing for each preset habitat. "Ask Airburn" answers your own questions live and writes a briefing for any values you set, citing the findings it used.

4. Predicts. Models fitted to every FLEX droplet test (261) and every lit CFI-G gas flame (132) predict, at your exact conditions, the chance a flame goes out on its own, burns until the fuel is used up or the droplet disrupts, the burning rate, and the oxygen level where going out on its own becomes a 50-50 chance. Each prediction carries a 90% range from 300 bootstrap refits. A simulation plays 60 model droplets next to the real tests nearest your oxygen level.

5. Replays NASA's tests. 256 FLEX droplet tests and 179 CFI-G gas-flame tests play back in time-lapse: each droplet starts at its recorded size, shrinks by the d² law and ends at its recorded burn time, the way the table says it ended.

6. Shows where the data ends. An oxygen-against-pressure map places 754 tests and 8 crew atmospheres. Saffire-II's paired microgravity and normal-gravity burns show how much gravity changed each outcome (it flipped 4 of 9 samples), which NASA's challenge statement says could bound the Moon and Mars. The site then shows NASA's own drop-tower tests at Moon and Mars gravity, from a NASA report: for three materials' oxygen limits, the bound did not hold.

7. Compares investigations by fuel, conditions, what varied and what was measured, and exports a brief with the exact test records behind it.

8. Goes beyond the PSI tables. Seven NASA technical reports hold results PSI lacks, and the site shows them beside the PSI results, never mixed in. Saffire IV to VI burned fabric and PMMA in a Cygnus cargo spacecraft at up to 31% oxygen and 7.8 psi; the PMMA fires pushed CO2 past NASA's 1-hour limit, and a tight smoke alarm would only have tripped at 981 s. The Shuttle's SSCE burned paper and PMMA at 35 to 70% oxygen. NASA Glenn drop-tower tests found Mylar, Ultem and Nomex all burning at lower oxygen at Moon gravity than on Earth or in microgravity (Mylar by 5.75 points; Nomex and Ultem went out at 21% oxygen on Earth and kept burning at 21% at Moon gravity). NASA White Sands tests show 7 of 26 material setups kept burning at Moon-base air in Earth gravity, and all 7 materials tested became flammable in pure oxygen above 0.4 to 0.9 psi, far below a spacesuit's 4.3 psi.

The trade-off, and how we checked it. The prebreathe side uses NASA's decompression index R: the nitrogen pressure in the body's slowest (360-minute) tissue divided by the suit pressure. NASA accepted the Shuttle and ISS prebreathe protocols at R = 1.65, and breathing pure oxygen halves that nitrogen every 360 minutes. The breathing side is inspired oxygen, the oxygen fraction times the pressure less 47 mmHg of water vapour, with NASA's exploration atmosphere (128 mmHg) setting the floor. The fire side is the FLEX droplet model. An automated check (tests/air.mjs) holds the physiology to NASA's published numbers: 4.3 hours of prebreathe from ISS air against NASA's 4-hour protocol, and, with a stricter limit set only from NASA's 2024 estimate of about 6.5 hours from sea-level air, the least-oxygen no-prebreathe cabin at 33.5% oxygen and 8.2 psi, next to the 34% and 8.2 psi NASA chose. A third check: with a 5.8 psi suit, the model's no-prebreathe cabin sits at 12.2 psi, next to the 11.8 psi cabin (R 1.6, no prebreathe) that the Shuttle suit's makers proposed with the same suit pressure. Under the stricter limit the suit helps less: a 5.8 psi suit's no-prebreathe cabin moves to 26.7%, and the burn line takes 6.9 psi. A suit curve on the home page shows what each suit pressure buys: in the least-oxygen cabin that needs no prebreathe, the model's chance that a methanol droplet flame goes out on its own rises from 14% at 4.3 psi to 50% at 5.3 psi and 67% at 5.8 psi (heptane: 4% to 36%). The estimate is simplified on purpose (one tissue, at rest) and labelled as an estimate, not test data.

The burn line, and how we checked it. We compared only tests with nothing added to the nitrogen, because CO2 and helium make flames go out more often. Every oxygen band in FLEX includes tests from about 10 to 15 psi, so oxygen and pressure are not confounded, and the model says Moon-base pressure moves the line by under 2 points. The model was scored on tests it never saw (5-fold cross-validation): it ranks flames that went out above those that did not with AUC 0.88 and names the right ending 78% of the time, against 69% for always guessing the commonest. It also learned, unprompted, that bigger droplets go out more often, consistent with large droplet flames losing more heat by radiation. CFI-G gas flames point the same way: at 18 to 23.4% oxygen all 41 lit flames went out on their own; at 33.2 to 40%, 30 of 91 burned until the fuel was cut off. Whether a gas flame lights at all could not be predicted better than guessing, so the site says so and does not predict it.

How SI is used, and checked. Code computes every number first; SI only interprets those facts. Two checks run on every SI text, at build time and live in the browser: code looks up every number in the facts and removes any sentence with a number that is not there, and a second model re-reads each sentence against the facts and removes any it judges unsupported. Every precomputed text was then read in full as a third check, because early versions passed both checks while wrong; one such briefing was discarded and regenerated.

Built so it can be checked. Every record links to its NASA PSI page, and the original NASA text sits beside every converted value. Every number from a NASA report names the report, table and page, and the build recomputes the partial-gravity report's printed margins from the transcribed limits. Where a table is silent, the cell stays empty; nothing is estimated. 195 automated checks confirm the site's JavaScript gives the same rankings and predictions as the Python that built them, and a sweep of 10,860 slider settings checks the ranking.

Benefits. Engineers can see how close the evidence comes to a cabin design before choosing its air; researchers get one clean table and fitted models to build on; students can see NASA's experiments run. On Earth, the same questions sit behind the fine-water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection and firefighter gear the challenge statement names; the catalog includes the SAME and SAME-R smoke tests and the FLEX tests with CO2 and helium added.

Limits. Airburn is an evidence summary, not a safety assessment. The models cover only the conditions tested, and droplets and gas flames in a test chamber are not cabin materials; the tests changed several things at once, so the findings are patterns, not proven causes. 21 PSI tables are loaded, every experiment table PSI offers for its flight combustion investigations. No PSI test ran in Moon or Mars gravity; the drop-tower tests from NASA's report last about 5 seconds, and NASA's standard material tests ran in Earth gravity.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn) for the data pipeline and models; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for a static site on GitHub Pages; Google Gemini models through a Google Apps Script proxy for live SI; Node.js for the automated checks.
